COURSE CODE 1BECL306LABORATORY MANUAL

Analog Electronics and Linear Integrated Circuit Lab

Design, circuit diagrams, procedure, observation tables, model graphs and viva questions for all twelve experiments. Every value in the design sections is worked out so that the circuit can be built and tested in one lab session.

Part A · Fixed experiments

  1. A1BJT common-emitter amplifier with and without feedback
  2. A2BJT Colpitts and crystal oscillators
  3. A3BJT Darlington emitter follower
  4. A44-bit R-2R op-amp DAC
  5. A5Second-order active low‑pass and high‑pass filters
  6. A6Precision half-wave and full-wave rectifiers
  7. A7Monostable and astable multivibrators using the 555
  8. A8Regulated power supply using 7805 and 7905

Part B · Open-ended experiments

  1. B1FET voltage-series feedback amplifier
  2. B2Class-C tuned amplifier
  3. B3Schmitt trigger for given UTP and LTP
  4. B4Sample-and-hold circuit

Before you start

Laboratory instructions

Preparation

  • Read the theory and complete the design section before the lab. Bring the design values, a semi-log graph sheet and the observation tables drawn in your record.
  • The designs assume typical device values (β=100 for the BJT, IDSS≈10 mA and VP≈−4 V for the JFET, ±Vsat≈±10 V for the 741). Measure your own devices where the procedure asks for it and redo the design with the measured values.
  • Circuit diagrams show IC pin numbers beside each lead. Check them against the pin-out table in the appendix before switching on.

Wiring and power

  • Set the power-supply voltage before connecting it, then switch off, wire the circuit and switch on again. Connect ground first and remove it last.
  • Op-amps and the 555 need their supply pins connected even when a textbook figure omits them. For the 741: +12 V to pin 7, −12 V to pin 4, and the supply ground to the circuit ground.
  • Electrolytic capacitors are polarised: the + lead goes to the more positive node (the diagrams mark it). A reversed electrolytic can overheat and burst.
  • Measure every resistor with the multimeter before inserting it. A wrong colour-code reading is the most common cause of a "dead" circuit.

Measuring

  • Use the CRO on DC coupling to check bias levels, and on AC coupling to measure small signals riding on a DC level. Use ×10 probes for high-impedance or high-frequency nodes.
  • Set the function-generator amplitude with the circuit connected; the generator's 50 Ω output drops the voltage under load.
  • Keep the input constant during a frequency-response run and re-check it at every few readings.
CautionExperiment A8 uses a mains transformer. Only the instructor connects the primary. Switch the mains off before touching the secondary wiring, and never probe the 230 V side.

Equipment common to all experiments

EquipmentSpecification
Regulated DC power supplyDual 0–30 V, 1 A, with a fixed 5 V output
Function generatorSine, square and triangle, 1 Hz–1 MHz, with TTL output and DC offset
Cathode-ray or digital oscilloscopeDual channel, 20 MHz or more, X-Y mode
Digital multimeter3½ digit, with diode and hFE test
Decade resistance box (DRB)1 Ω–1 MΩ, two numbers
Breadboard, probes and wiresSingle-strand 0.5 mm hook-up wire

Writing the record

For each experiment: aim, components, circuit diagram with values, design calculations, tabulated readings, graphs (frequency responses on semi-log sheets), calculations, result and the answers to the viva questions.

Used throughout

Measurement methods

Voltage gain in decibels

Av=Vo (p‑p)Vi (p‑p),Av (dB)=20log10Av

Frequency response and bandwidth

  1. Keep the input amplitude constant and vary the frequency over the range given in the experiment, taking more readings near the corners.
  2. Plot gain in dB on the linear axis against frequency on the log axis of a semi-log sheet.
  3. Take the flat mid-band gain Am and draw a horizontal line at Am−3 dB. Where it cuts the curve are the lower and upper cut-off frequencies fL and fH.
BW=fH−fL,GBW=Am×BW(Am as a ratio, not in dB)

Input and output impedance

Input impedance (half-voltage method). Connect DRB 1 in series with the input as in Fig. M.1. With DRB 1 at zero, note the voltage Vi′ at the amplifier input. Increase DRB 1 until Vi′ falls to half that value. The DRB setting is then equal to the input impedance Zi. Keep the output undistorted throughout.

Output impedance. Note the output voltage Vo(NL) with no load. Connect DRB 2 across the output and reduce it until the output falls to Vo(NL)/2; the DRB setting is the output impedance Zo. When Zo is very small, use any convenient load RL and calculate:

Zo=RL(Vo(NL)Vo(L)−1)

CRO in X-Y mode

Feed the circuit input to channel 1 (X) and the output to channel 2 (Y) and select X-Y mode. The screen then shows the transfer characteristic Vo versus Vi directly. This is used for the precision rectifiers and the Schmitt trigger.

Part A · Experiment 1

BJT common-emitter amplifier with and without feedback

DateBatchMarksSignature

Aim

To design and set up a BJT common-emitter voltage amplifier, with and without negative feedback, and to determine its voltage gain, bandwidth, input impedance and output impedance.

Components and equipment

#ItemSpecificationQty
1NPN transistorBC547 (or SL100 / 2N2222)1
2Resistors, ¼ W47 kΩ (R1), 10 kΩ (R2), 2.2 kΩ (RC), 560 Ω (RE), 10 kΩ (RL)1 each
3Electrolytic capacitors, 25 V10 µF (CC1, CC2), 100 µF (CE)2 + 1
4DC power supply0–30 V, set to 12 V1
5Function generator, CRO, DMMsee general equipment list1 each
6Decade resistance boxfor Zi and Zo2

Theory

In the common-emitter (CE) configuration the input is applied between base and emitter and the output is taken between collector and emitter. A small change in base current produces a β-times larger change in collector current, and the collector resistor turns it into a large output voltage. The output is 180° out of phase with the input.

The voltage-divider bias R1–R2 fixes the base voltage. The emitter resistor RE provides DC negative feedback, which holds the operating point steady against changes in β and temperature. For signals, RE would also reduce the gain, so it is bypassed by CE. The mid-band gain is then set by the collector load and the dynamic emitter resistance re:

re=26mVIE Av≈−RC∥RLre(CE connected, no feedback)

At low frequencies the coupling capacitors and CE no longer act as short circuits, so the gain falls below the lower cut-off fL. At high frequencies the transistor's junction capacitances (magnified by the Miller effect) shunt the signal and the gain falls above fH.

With feedback. When CE is removed, the whole of RE carries the signal current. The voltage across RE, proportional to the output current, is subtracted from the input: this is current-series (series-series) negative feedback. The gain drops, but it becomes almost independent of β, the bandwidth increases, the input impedance rises and distortion falls. The gain–bandwidth product stays roughly constant.

Avf≈−RC∥RLre+RE Zi=R1∥R2∥β(re+RE),Zo≈RC

Design

Given VCC=12 V, IC=2 mA, β=100, lower cut-off fL≈100 Hz.

  1. Place the operating point in the middle of the load line and give RE a tenth of the supply for bias stability.VCE=VCC2=6V,VE=VCC10=1.2V
  2. Emitter resistor.RE=VEIE=1.2V2mA=600Ω→use 560Ω
  3. Collector resistor.RC=VCC−VCE−VEIC=12−6−1.22mA=2.4kΩ→use 2.2kΩ
  4. Base divider, with ten times the base current flowing through R2.VB=VE+VBE=1.2+0.7=1.9V,IB=ICβ=20µA R2=VB10IB=1.9V0.2mA=9.5kΩ→use 10kΩ R1=VCC−VB11IB=10.1V0.22mA=45.9kΩ→use 47kΩ
  5. Check with the chosen values, using the Thevenin equivalent of the divider.VTH=VCCR2R1+R2=12×1057=2.1V,RTH=R1∥R2=8.25kΩ IB=VTH−VBERTH+(β+1)RE=2.1−0.78.25kΩ+101×560Ω=21.7µA IC≈2.17mA,VCE≈6.0V✓
  6. Small-signal values.re=26mV2.19mA≈12Ω,βre≈1.2kΩ,Rin=R1∥R2∥βre≈1.05kΩ
  7. Bypass capacitor, with XCE=RE/10 at fL.CE=12πfL(RE/10)=12π×100×56≈28µF→use 100µF A larger value only lowers fL.
  8. Coupling capacitors, with XC=Rin/10 at fL.CC1=12π×100×105≈15µF→10µF is adequate (its own corner≈15Hz),CC2=10µF
  9. Expected mid-band gain with RL=10 kΩ, so that RC∥RL=1.8 kΩ.Av≈−1.8kΩ12Ω≈−150(43.5dB)without feedback Avf≈−1.8kΩ12Ω+560Ω≈−3.2(10dB)with feedback Zi≈1.05kΩ (without),≈7.2kΩ (with);Zo≈2.2kΩ

Circuit diagram

Procedure

  1. Check the transistor with the multimeter's diode or hFE range and measure all resistors.
  2. Wire the circuit of Fig. A1.1 with CE in place and RL=10 kΩ.
  3. DC check. With no signal, switch on 12 V and measure VB, VE and VC. Calculate VCE=VC−VE and IC=(VCC−VC)/RC. VCE should be close to 6 V.
  4. Apply Vi=20 mV p‑p at 1 kHz. Observe Vi and Vo on the two CRO channels: Vo must be an undistorted sine, inverted with respect to Vi. Reduce Vi if the output clips.
  5. Without feedback. Keeping Vi at 20 mV p‑p, vary the frequency from 50 Hz to 1 MHz and note Vo (Table A1.1).
  6. With feedback. Remove CE, raise Vi to 500 mV p‑p and repeat the frequency run (Table A1.2).
  7. Plot both responses on one semi-log sheet. Find Am, fL, fH, the bandwidth and the gain–bandwidth product.
  8. At 1 kHz, measure Zi and Zo by the half-voltage method, with and without CE.

Viva voce

  1. Why is the CE configuration preferred for voltage amplification?
  2. What does the emitter bypass capacitor do, and what happens when it is removed?
  3. Which type of feedback does an unbypassed RE give? How does it change gain, bandwidth, Zi and Zo?
  4. Which components set fL, and what sets fH?
  5. Why is the Q-point placed near VCE=VCC/2?
  6. Why is the output 180° out of phase with the input?
  7. Define bandwidth and gain–bandwidth product. Why is the product roughly constant?
  8. What is the Miller effect?

Part A · Experiment 2

BJT Colpitts oscillator and crystal oscillator

DateBatchMarksSignature

Aim

To design and set up (i) a BJT Colpitts oscillator and (ii) a BJT crystal oscillator, and to measure their frequency of oscillation.

Components and equipment

#ItemSpecificationQty
1NPN transistorBC547 (fT≈300 MHz)1
2Resistors, ¼ W47 kΩ, 10 kΩ, 2.2 kΩ, 560 Ω1 each
3Electrolytic capacitor100 µF / 25 V (CE)1
4Capacitors, Colpitts1 µF ×2 (coupling), 0.01 µF (C1), 0.1 µF (C2)4
5Inductor1 mH (or a decade inductance box)1
6Capacitors, crystal oscillator0.1 µF ×2 (coupling), 100 pF (C1), 1 nF (C2)4
7Quartz crystal4 MHz, HC-49 can1
8DC supply, CRO12 V; CRO ≥ 20 MHz (a frequency counter helps)1 each

Theory

An oscillator is an amplifier that supplies its own input through a positive-feedback network. Oscillations build up from noise and settle at the frequency where the Barkhausen criterion holds:

|Aβ|=1andtotal phase shift around the loop=0° (or 360°)

In practice |Aβ| is made slightly greater than 1 so that oscillations start; the transistor's non-linearity then limits the amplitude.

Colpitts oscillator. The CE amplifier gives 180° of phase shift. The tank circuit, an inductor L with a capacitive divider C1–C2, forms a π network that gives the other 180° at its resonant frequency. The tapped capacitors also set the feedback fraction:

fo=12πLCeq,Ceq=C1C2C1+C2 β=C1C2,so the amplifier gain must satisfy |A|≥C2C1

Here C1 is on the collector side and C2 on the base side. With C2/C1=10 a single CE stage easily meets the gain condition. The same tank works with a JFET common-source stage (BFW10) in place of the BJT.

Crystal oscillator. A quartz crystal is piezoelectric: a voltage across it makes it vibrate mechanically, and the vibration produces a voltage. Electrically it behaves like a series RLC branch (the motional arm L, C, R) shunted by the holder capacitance Cm. It has two resonances very close together:

fs=12πLC(series),fp=12πLCCmC+Cm(parallel, slightly above fs)

Between fs and fp the crystal is inductive, so it can replace L in the Colpitts circuit. Its Q is 104 to 106, far higher than any LC tank, so the frequency hardly depends on the transistor, supply or temperature. The circuit oscillates within a few parts per million of the frequency marked on the crystal.

Design

Colpitts oscillator, fo≈50 kHz

  1. Bias the CE stage exactly as in Experiment A1 (IC≈2 mA, VCE≈6 V).R1=47kΩ,R2=10kΩ,RC=2.2kΩ,RE=560Ω,CE=100µF
  2. Choose the tank capacitors with C2/C1=10, well within hfe.C1=0.01µF,C2=0.1µF→Ceq=0.01×0.10.11µF=9.09nF
  3. Inductance for 50 kHz.L=14π2fo2Ceq=14π2×(50×103)2×9.09×10−9=1.11mH→use 1mH
  4. Frequency with the chosen values.fo=12π1×10−3×9.09×10−9=52.8kHz
  5. Coupling capacitors must be short circuits at fo.CC=1µF→XC=12π×52.8kHz×1µF≈3Ω

Crystal oscillator, 4 MHz

  1. Same bias network. Replace L by the crystal and scale the capacitors for megahertz operation, keeping C2/C1=10.C1=100pF,C2=1nF,CC=0.1µF(XC≈0.4Ω at 4MHz)
  2. The frequency is set by the crystal, not by C1 and C2.fo≈4MHz (marked value), slightly above fs

Circuit diagrams

Procedure

  1. Wire the Colpitts oscillator of Fig. A2.1. Switch on 12 V and check the bias: VCE≈6 V.
  2. Connect the CRO to Vo. A stable sine wave should appear. If it does not start, check the tank connections and the ratio C2/C1.
  3. Measure the period T and calculate fo=1/T. Note the peak-to-peak amplitude.
  4. Change L (or C1 and C2 together) as in Table A2.1 and repeat. Compare each measured frequency with the calculated one.
  5. Wire the crystal oscillator of Fig. A2.2. Observe Vo and measure the frequency, using a frequency counter if the CRO time base is too coarse. Compare with the value marked on the crystal.

Part A · Experiment 3

BJT Darlington emitter follower

DateBatchMarksSignature

Aim

To realise a BJT Darlington emitter follower and determine its voltage gain, input impedance and output impedance.

Components and equipment

#ItemSpecificationQty
1NPN transistorsBC547 ×2 (or BC547 driving an SL100)2
2Resistors, ¼ W47 kΩ (R1), 82 kΩ (R2), 1.2 kΩ (RE), 1 kΩ (RL)1 each
3Electrolytic capacitors, 25 V10 µF (Cin), 100 µF (Cout)1 each
4DC supply, function generator, CRO, DMM12 V1 each
5Decade resistance boxfor Zi and Zo2

Theory

In a Darlington pair the emitter current of Q1 is the base current of Q2 and the collectors are tied together. The pair behaves like one transistor with a very large current gain and twice the base-emitter drop:

βD≈β1β2(≈104 for two β=100 devices),VBE(D)=VBE1+VBE2≈1.4V

Used as an emitter follower (common collector), the output taken from the emitter of Q2 follows the input with a gain just below one and no phase inversion. The whole output voltage opposes the input between base and emitter: this is voltage-series feedback with β=1. The result is a very high input impedance and a very low output impedance, so the circuit is used as a buffer between a high-impedance source and a low-impedance load.

Av=RE′RE′+re2+re1/β2≈1,RE′=RE∥RL Zi=R1∥R2∥βDRE′(the bias divider dominates) Zo≈re2+re1+Rs′/β1β2,Rs′=Rs∥R1∥R2,Ai≈βD

Because βDRE′ is several megaohms, the input impedance is set almost entirely by R1∥R2. Bootstrapping the divider can raise it further.

Design

Given VCC=12 V, IE2=5 mA, β1=β2=100.

  1. Place the output at half the supply for the largest symmetrical swing.VE2=VCC2=6V→RE=6V5mA=1.2kΩ
  2. The base of Q1 sits two VBE drops above the output.VB1=VE2+2VBE=6+1.4=7.4V
  3. The base current is tiny, so choose R1 and set R2 for VB1.IB1=IE2β1β2≈0.5µA R2=R1VB1VCC−VB1=47kΩ×7.44.6=75.6kΩ→use 82kΩ then VB1=7.63V,VE2=6.23V,IE2=5.2mA
  4. Dynamic resistances.re2=26mV5.2mA=5Ω,IE1=IE2β2=52µA→re1=500Ω
  5. Expected performance with RL=1 kΩ, so that RE′=545 Ω.Av≈545545+5+5≈0.98 Zi≈47kΩ∥82kΩ≈30kΩ,Zo≈5+500+50/100100≈10Ω
  6. Coupling capacitors. Cout must be large because the output impedance is only about 10 Ω.Cin=10µF(corner with 30kΩ≈0.5Hz),Cout=100µF(XC≈1.6Ω at 1kHz)

Circuit diagram

Procedure

  1. Wire the circuit of Fig. A3.1. With no input, measure VB1, VE1 and VE2: expect about 7.6 V, 6.9 V and 6.2 V.
  2. Apply Vi=1 V p‑p at 1 kHz. Observe Vi and Vo together: they are in phase and almost equal.
  3. Measure Vo and calculate Av=Vo/Vi. Optionally repeat from 50 Hz to 1 MHz to check the bandwidth.
  4. Zi. Insert DRB 1 in series with the input and increase it until the voltage after the DRB falls to half. Zi equals the DRB setting (about 30 kΩ).
  5. Zo. Reduce Vi to 100 mV p‑p so that the follower is not overdriven by a heavy load. Note Vo with RL removed, then connect RL=100 Ω (or a DRB) and note Vo again. Calculate Zo=RL(Vo(NL)/Vo(L)−1).

  2. What are the advantages and disadvantages of a Darlington pair?
  3. Why is the voltage gain of an emitter follower slightly less than one?
  4. Why is the measured input impedance much smaller than βDRE?

Part A · Experiment 4

4-bit R-2R ladder digital-to-analog converter

DateBatchMarksSignature

Aim

To design a 4-bit R-2R ladder DAC using an op-amp and test it (i) with a 4-bit binary input set by toggle switches and (ii) with digital inputs generated by a mod-16 counter.

Components and equipment

#ItemSpecificationQty
1Op-ampµA7411
2Binary counter (part II)7493 / 74LS931
3Resistors, ¼ W, 1 % if available10 kΩ ×4 (R, Rf), 20 kΩ ×5 (2R)9
4SPDT toggle switchesor jumper wires to +5 V / ground4
5Power supplies±12 V (op-amp), +5 V (reference and 7493)1 set
6Function generatorTTL output, 1 kHz (part II)1
7CRO, DMM—1 each

Theory

A digital-to-analog converter produces an output voltage proportional to the value of a binary input word. The binary-weighted resistor DAC needs a different resistor for every bit, which is hard to match for more than a few bits. The R-2R ladder uses only two values, R and 2R, so it is easy to build accurately.

Each bit drives a ladder node through 2R, the nodes are joined by R, and the LSB end is terminated in 2R. From any node, the resistance looking towards the LSB end is 2R, so every node splits current equally and each bit's contribution is halved at every node towards the output. The ladder is equivalent to a source of resistance R with an open-circuit voltage

Vth=VR(D32+D24+D18+D016)=VRD16,Rth=R

where D is the decimal value of D3D2D1D0 and VR is the logic-1 level. Connected to the virtual ground of an inverting amplifier with feedback resistor Rf:

Vo=−RfR·VRD16 Resolution (1 LSB)=RfR·VR16,Full scale=15 LSB

Important specifications are resolution, accuracy (error from ideal), linearity, monotonicity and settling time.

With a counter. The 7493 contains a divide-by-2 section (input A, output QA) and a divide-by-8 section (input B, outputs QB, QC, QD). Joining QA to input B makes a 4-bit ripple counter that counts 0000 to 1111 on the falling edges of the clock at input A. Fed to the ladder, the count produces a 16-step staircase that repeats every 16 clock periods.

Design

  1. Logic levels: logic 1 = VR = +5 V, logic 0 = 0 V.
  2. Ladder resistors, large enough not to load the logic outputs.R=10kΩ,2R=20kΩ
  3. Feedback resistor Rf=R.Vo=−5×D16V→resolution=0.3125V,full scale (1111)=−4.6875V
  4. Check that the op-amp does not saturate: 4.7 V is well inside ±10 V with ±12 V supplies. For larger steps use Rf=2R.Rf=20kΩ→steps of 0.625V,full scale −9.375V

Circuit diagrams

Procedure

Part I · switch inputs

  1. Wire Fig. A4.1. Connect +12 V to pin 7 and −12 V to pin 4 of the 741. The A throw of each switch goes to +5 V, the B throw to ground.
  2. Set the switches to each combination from 0000 to 1111. Measure Vo with the DMM and record it in Table A4.1.
  3. Plot Vo against the decimal input D. It should be a straight line through the origin with slope −0.3125 V per step. Note the largest deviation from the line.

Part II · counter inputs

  1. Wire Fig. A4.2. Supply the 7493 with +5 V at pin 5 and ground at pin 10. Ground the reset inputs R0(1) and R0(2) (pins 2 and 3). Join QA (pin 12) to input B (pin 1).
  2. Feed a 1 kHz TTL clock to input A (pin 14). The outputs QA, QB, QC, QD drive the 2R resistors from LSB to MSB.
  3. View the clock and Vo on the CRO with DC coupling. Vo is a staircase of 16 steps that falls from 0 V to full scale and returns to 0 V every 16 clock periods. Measure the step height and full-scale value.
TTL outputs give about 3.4 V for logic 1, not 5 V, so the staircase steps are smaller than in part I. Use the measured high level in place of VR when comparing with theory.

Maximum linearity error: . With the counter, a 16-step staircase was obtained.

Part A · Experiment 5

Second-order active low‑pass and high‑pass filters

DateBatchMarksSignature

Aim

To design and test second-order Butterworth active filters for a cut-off frequency of 1 kHz, (i) low‑pass and (ii) high‑pass, and to plot their frequency responses.

Components and equipment

#ItemSpecificationQty
1Op-ampµA7411
2Resistors, ¼ W16 kΩ ×2 (R), 10 kΩ (R1), 5.6 kΩ + 270 Ω in series (Rf = 5.86 kΩ)5
3Capacitors0.01 µF, polyester or ceramic2
4Power supply±12 V1
5Function generator, CRO—1 each

Theory

Active filters combine RC networks with an op-amp. They need no inductors, can have gain, and their high input and low output impedance let stages be cascaded without loading. A second-order filter rolls off at 40 dB/decade beyond the cut-off frequency, twice as fast as a single RC section.

The Sallen-Key (voltage-controlled voltage-source) circuit uses a non-inverting amplifier of gain A0=1+Rf/R1 and two RC sections, one of them returned to the output. With equal resistors R and equal capacitors C:

Low-pass:H(s)=A0ωc2s2+(3−A0)ωcs+ωc2 High-pass:H(s)=A0s2s2+(3−A0)ωcs+ωc2 fc=12πRC,Q=13−A0

The Butterworth response is maximally flat in the passband. It needs Q=0.707 (damping 1.414), so the gain must be A0=3−1.414=1.586. At fc the gain is 3 dB below the passband gain: 0.707×1.586=1.12, which is +1 dB. If A0 reached 3, the circuit would oscillate.

The high‑pass filter is obtained from the low‑pass by exchanging the positions of R and C (the RC–CR transformation).

Design

  1. Cut-off frequency fc=1 kHz. Choose C=0.01 µF.R=12πfcC=12π×1000×0.01×10−6=15.9kΩ→use 16kΩ(fc=995Hz)
  2. Butterworth gain.A0=1+RfR1=1.586→Rf=0.586R1;R1=10kΩ→Rf=5.86kΩ(5.6kΩ+270Ω)
  3. High-pass: interchange R and C, keeping the same values.fc=995Hz,passband gain 1.586(4dB)

Circuit diagrams

Procedure

  1. Wire the low‑pass filter of Fig. A5.1 with ±12 V on pins 7 and 4.
  2. Apply Vi=1 V p‑p sine. Vary the frequency from 10 Hz to 100 kHz and note Vo (Table A5.1). Keep Vi constant.
  3. Calculate the gain in dB and plot it against frequency on a semi-log sheet. Find the passband gain, the cut-off frequency at 3 dB below it, and the roll-off from two readings a decade apart above fc.
  4. Wire the high‑pass filter of Fig. A5.2 and repeat (Table A5.2).
Above about 50 kHz the 741's slew rate (0.5 V/µs) starts to distort a large high‑pass output. Keep Vi at 1 V p‑p or less.

Part A · Experiment 6

Precision half-wave and full-wave rectifiers

DateBatchMarksSignature

Aim

To design and test op-amp precision rectifiers: (i) a half-wave precision rectifier and (ii) a full-wave precision rectifier.

Components and equipment

#ItemSpecificationQty
1Op-ampsµA741 (TL081 or LF356 for higher frequencies)2
2Signal diodes1N41482
3Resistors, ¼ W10 kΩ ×7; 5 kΩ ×1 (or two 10 kΩ in parallel)8
4Power supply±12 V1
5Function generator, CROdual channel, X-Y mode1 each

Theory

An ordinary diode rectifier does not conduct until the input exceeds its cut-in voltage of about 0.6–0.7 V, so it cannot rectify small signals and it distorts larger ones. A precision rectifier places the diode inside the feedback loop of an op-amp. The op-amp output moves by whatever is needed to forward-bias the diode, so the effective cut-in voltage is divided by the open-loop gain:

Vγ(eff)=VγAOL=0.7V2×105≈3.5µV

The combination behaves like an ideal diode, often called a super diode.

Half-wave rectifier (Fig. A6.1)

  • Vi positive: the op-amp output swings negative and D1 conducts. It clamps the output at about −0.7 V and holds the inverting input at virtual ground. D2 is reverse-biased and Vo=0.
  • Vi negative: the output swings positive. D2 conducts, D1 is off, and the circuit is an inverting amplifier with Vo=−(Rf/R1)Vi, which is positive.

So the output is a positive half-wave that follows the negative half-cycles of the input. D1 also keeps the op-amp out of saturation on the other half-cycle, which lets it respond faster.

Full-wave rectifier (absolute-value circuit, Fig. A6.2)

Stage U1 is a half-wave rectifier with the diodes reversed. It gives V1=−Vi for positive inputs and V1=0 for negative inputs. Stage U2 is an inverting summer that adds Vi with weight 1 and V1 with weight 2 (R4=R/2):

Vo=−(Vi+2V1) Vi>0:V1=−Vi→Vo=−(Vi−2Vi)=+Vi Vi<0:V1=0→Vo=−Vi=|Vi|

Hence Vo=|Vi|: a full-wave rectified output with no diode drop. The main limitation is the op-amp slew rate, which rounds the output near each zero crossing at higher frequencies.

Design

  1. Unity gain for the half-wave rectifier.R1=Rf=10kΩ,RL=10kΩ
  2. Full-wave rectifier: equal resistors except the summing weight of V1.R1=R2=R3=R5=10kΩ,R4=R2=5kΩ
  3. Diodes: fast-switching signal diodes, 1N4148 (trr≈4 ns).
  4. Frequency limit: at each zero crossing the 741 output must slew about 1.4 V (two diode drops).t≈1.4V0.5V/µs≈3µs→keep f≤5kHz for a clean output

Circuit diagrams

Procedure

  1. Wire the half-wave rectifier of Fig. A6.1.
  2. Apply Vi=1 V p‑p at 1 kHz. Observe Vi and Vo on the CRO with DC coupling and sketch both waveforms with their peak values.
  3. Reduce Vi to 200 mV p‑p and confirm that it is still rectified without loss, which a plain diode cannot do.
  4. Switch the CRO to X-Y mode (Vi on X, Vo on Y) and sketch the transfer characteristic.
  5. Wire the full-wave rectifier of Fig. A6.2 and repeat steps 2–4.
  6. Optionally raise the frequency to 10 kHz and 50 kHz and note the distortion near zero crossings.

Part A · Experiment 7

Monostable and astable multivibrators using the 555 timer

DateBatchMarksSignature

Aim

To design and test using the 555 timer (i) a monostable multivibrator with a pulse width of 1.1 ms and (ii) an astable multivibrator with a frequency of 1 kHz and a duty cycle of 60 %.

Components and equipment

#ItemSpecificationQty
1Timer ICNE5551
2Resistors, ¼ W10 kΩ ×2 (R, R2), 2.7 kΩ (RA), 5.6 kΩ (RB)4
3Capacitors0.1 µF ×2 (C, C1), 0.01 µF ×2 (CT, control pin)4
4Diode1N41481
5Power supply+5 V1
6Function generator, CROsquare wave for the trigger1 each

Theory

Inside the 555 a chain of three 5 kΩ resistors sets two reference levels, 23VCC and 13VCC. The threshold comparator (pin 6) resets an SR flip-flop when its input rises above 23VCC. The trigger comparator (pin 2) sets it when its input falls below 13VCC. The flip-flop drives the output (pin 3) and a discharge transistor (pin 7) that shorts the timing capacitor while the output is low. Pin 5 gives access to the 23VCC reference and is decoupled with 0.01 µF. Pin 4 (reset) is tied to VCC when not used.

Monostable (one-shot)

In the stable state the output is low and the discharge transistor holds C discharged. A negative trigger pulse at pin 2 (below VCC/3) sets the flip-flop: the output goes high, pin 7 releases C, and C charges through R towards VCC. When VC reaches 23VCC the threshold comparator resets the flip-flop, the output returns low and C is discharged. The pulse width depends only on R and C:

T=RCln3≈1.1RC

The trigger must be shorter than T and must return high before the pulse ends, so the square-wave trigger is differentiated by CT and R2 into short negative spikes. D1 clips the positive spikes to VCC.

Astable (free-running)

C1 charges through RA+RB from 13VCC to 23VCC while the output is high, then discharges through RB into pin 7 while the output is low. The cycle repeats with no trigger:

tH=0.693(RA+RB)C1,tL=0.693RBC1 T=tH+tL=0.693(RA+2RB)C1,f=1.44(RA+2RB)C1 D=tHT=RA+RBRA+2RB(always above 50%)

A duty cycle below 50 % needs a diode across RB, so that C1 charges through RA alone.

Design

Monostable, T=1.1 ms, VCC=5 V

  1. Choose C=0.1 µF.R=T1.1C=1.1ms1.1×0.1µF=10kΩ
  2. Trigger differentiator, much faster than T.CT=0.01µF,R2=10kΩ→τ=R2CT=0.1ms≪1.1ms
  3. Trigger source: a 0–5 V square wave whose period exceeds T.ftrig=500Hz→period=2ms>T

Astable, f=1 kHz, D=60 %, VCC=5 V

  1. Split the period.T=1ms→tH=0.6ms,tL=0.4ms
  2. Choose C1=0.1 µF.RB=tL0.693C1=0.4ms0.693×0.1µF=5.77kΩ→use 5.6kΩ RA=tH0.693C1−RB=8.66kΩ−5.77kΩ=2.89kΩ→use 2.7kΩ
  3. Check with the standard values.tH=0.693×8.3kΩ×0.1µF=0.575ms,tL=0.693×5.6kΩ×0.1µF=0.388ms T=0.963ms→f=1.04kHz,D=59.7%

Circuit diagrams

Procedure

Monostable

  1. Wire Fig. A7.1 with VCC=5 V on pins 8 and 4.
  2. Apply a 500 Hz, 0–5 V square wave at Vtrig. Observe the trigger at pin 2, the output at pin 3 and the capacitor voltage VC at pins 6 and 7.
  3. Measure the output pulse width T and the peak of VC (it should stop at 23VCC≈3.3 V). Compare T with 1.1RC.
  4. Repeat with other values of R or C (Table A7.1).

Astable

  1. Wire Fig. A7.2.
  2. Observe Vo (pin 3) and VC (pins 2 and 6) together. VC should swing between about 1.67 V and 3.33 V.
  3. Measure tH, tL and T. Calculate f and the duty cycle and compare with the design (Table A7.2).
  4. Repeat with another pair of RA and RB.

Part A · Experiment 8

Regulated power supply using IC 7805 and IC 7905

DateBatchMarksSignature

Aim

To design and test a regulated dual power supply of ±5 V using the fixed regulators 7805 and 7905, and to determine the line and load regulation.

Components and equipment

#ItemSpecificationQty
1Step-down transformer230 V / 12-0-12 V, 500 mA, centre-tapped1
2Rectifier diodes1N4007 (1000 V, 1 A)4
3Electrolytic capacitors1000 µF / 25 V ×2, 2.2 µF / 25 V, 1 µF / 25 V4
4Ceramic capacitors0.33 µF, 0.1 µF2
5Regulators7805, 7905 (TO-220, with small heat sinks)1 each
6Fuse500 mA with holder1
7Loaddecade resistance box, or 100 Ω–1 kΩ rated at 1 W or more1
8MetersDMM ×2 (or a 0–100 mA ammeter and a voltmeter)2
9Variable DC supply0–30 V, for the line-regulation test1
10CROfor ripple1

Theory

A DC power supply is built in four stages: a transformer steps the mains down, a rectifier converts AC to pulsating DC, a filter capacitor smooths it, and a regulator holds the output constant against changes in mains voltage and load current.

With a centre-tapped secondary and a bridge rectifier, the two DC corners of the bridge give a positive and a negative voltage with respect to the centre tap. Each half behaves as a full-wave rectifier, so the ripple is at 100 Hz.

Vm=2×12V=16.97V,VDC≈Vm−VD≈16.3V(no load) Vr(p‑p)≈IL2fC(full-wave, capacitor filter)

Three-terminal regulators. The 78xx series gives a fixed positive output (7805: +5 V), the 79xx series a fixed negative output (7905: −5 V). Inside are a voltage reference, an error amplifier, a series pass transistor, current limiting, thermal shutdown and safe-area protection. They need the input at least 2 V beyond the output (the dropout voltage), so a 7805 needs 7 V or more. The maximum input is 35 V.

Pin-outs differ7805: pin 1 input, 2 ground, 3 output. 7905: pin 1 ground, 2 input, 3 output. Swapping them destroys the regulator.

The input capacitor (0.33 µF for the 7805, 2.2 µF for the 7905) keeps the regulator stable when it is far from the filter capacitor. The output capacitor improves the response to sudden load changes.

Line regulation=ΔVoΔVin(mV/V),orΔVo/VoΔVin×100(%/V) Load regulation=VNL−VFLVFL×100%

Design

  1. Outputs ±5 V at up to IL=100 mA each.
  2. The 12-0-12 V transformer gives about 16.3 V peak on each rail, well above the 7 V the regulator needs.
  3. Filter capacitor for no more than 2 V p‑p ripple at 100 mA.C=IL2fVr=0.12×50×2=500µF→use 1000µF(Vr≈1V) lowest input≈16.3−1=15.3V≫7V✓
  4. The diode peak inverse voltage in this circuit is about 2Vm.PIV≈34V→1N4007 (1000 V, 1 A)✓
  5. Regulator dissipation at full load.P=(16.3−5)V×0.1A≈1.1W→use small heat sinks

Circuit diagrams

Procedure

CautionThe transformer primary is at 230 V. The instructor connects the mains and the fuse. Switch off before changing any secondary wiring.

Part I · complete dual supply

  1. With the mains off, wire the secondary side of Fig. A8.1. Check the polarity of every electrolytic and the regulator pin-outs.
  2. Switch on. Measure the unregulated DC across C1 and C2 and the regulated outputs +5 V and −5 V with the DMM.
  3. With a load of about 100 Ω on each output, view the ripple at the filter capacitor and at the regulator output on the CRO (AC coupling). Note both ripple amplitudes.

Part II · line and load regulation of the 7805

  1. Wire Fig. A8.2, feeding the 7805 from the variable DC supply.
  2. Line regulation. Set RL=100 Ω (IL≈50 mA). Raise Vin from 0 to 20 V in 1 V steps and note Vo (Table A8.1). Plot Vo against Vin: regulation starts at about 7 V.
  3. Load regulation. Set Vin=10 V. Note Vo with no load, then with RL = 1 kΩ, 500 Ω, 250 Ω, 150 Ω and 100 Ω, recording IL each time (Table A8.2). Plot Vo against IL.
  4. Optionally repeat part II for the 7905 with a negative input.

Part B · Open-ended experiment 1

FET voltage-series feedback amplifier

DateBatchMarksSignature

Aim

To design a JFET voltage-series feedback amplifier (common-drain source follower) and determine its voltage gain, input impedance and output impedance.

Components and equipment

#ItemSpecificationQty
1N-channel JFETBFW10 (or BFW11)1
2Resistors, ¼ W1 MΩ ×2 (RG1, RG2), 3.9 kΩ (RS), 10 kΩ (RL)4
3Capacitors0.1 µF (Cin), 10 µF / 25 V electrolytic (Cout)2
4DC supply0–30 V (12 V), plus a second channel for measuring IDSS and VP1
5Function generator, CRO (×10 probe), DMM, DRB—1 each

Theory

Negative feedback returns part of the output to the input in opposition to it. In voltage-series (series-shunt) feedback, the output voltage is sampled (the feedback network is in parallel with the output) and the feedback voltage is placed in series with the input. For open-loop gain A and feedback fraction β:

Af=A1+Aβ,D=1+Aβ(desensitivity) Zif=Zi(1+Aβ),Zof=Zo1+Aβ

So this type of feedback raises the input impedance, lowers the output impedance, widens the bandwidth, reduces distortion and makes the gain insensitive to device parameters.

In the common-drain JFET amplifier the output is taken across RS, and the gate-source voltage is Vgs=Vi−Vo. The entire output voltage is fed back in series with the input, so β=1. The open-loop gain is the transconductance times the source load:

A=gmRS′,RS′=RS∥RL Af=gmRS′1+gmRS′<1(in phase) Zi≈RG1∥RG2,Zo=RS∥1gm

The JFET follows the square law, and its transconductance falls as VGS approaches pinch-off:

ID=IDSS(1−VGSVP)2,gm=gm0(1−VGSVP),gm0=2IDSS|VP|

Because the gate draws almost no current, the input impedance is set by the bias resistors and can be made very high.

Design

Measure IDSS and VP of your JFET first (procedure step 1). The numbers below use typical BFW10 values IDSS=10 mA and VP=−4 V, with VDD=12 V and ID=2 mA.

  1. Gate-source voltage for the chosen drain current.VGS=VP(1−IDIDSS)=−4(1−0.2)=−2.21V
  2. Gate bias at half the supply, with very high divider resistors for a high Zi.RG1=RG2=1MΩ→VG=6V,Zi≈500kΩ
  3. Source resistor.VS=VG−VGS=6+2.21=8.21V→RS=VSID=4.1kΩ→use 3.9kΩ
  4. Check that the JFET is in saturation (pinch-off).VDS=12−8.2=3.8V>VGS−VP=1.8V✓
  5. Transconductance.gm0=2×10mA4V=5mS,gm=5mS×(1−2.214)=2.24mS
  6. Expected gain with RL=10 kΩ.RS′=3.9kΩ∥10kΩ=2.8kΩ→A=gmRS′=6.3,D=7.3 Af=6.37.3=0.86
  7. Output impedance.Zo=RS∥1gm=3.9kΩ∥446Ω≈400Ω
  8. Coupling capacitors.Cin=0.1µF(corner with 500kΩ≈3Hz),Cout=10µF
Open-ended options. Redesign for a different ID; return RG2 to a tap on a split source resistor (bootstrapping) to raise Zi into the megohms; or add a drain resistor and compare the common-source gain (no feedback) with this follower.

Circuit diagram

Procedure

  1. Device parameters. With gate and source grounded and VDS≈10 V, measure the drain current: this is IDSS. Make VGS more negative until ID is nearly zero (about 10 µA): this VGS is VP. Redo the design with these values.
  2. Wire the circuit of Fig. B1.1. Measure VG, VS and VDS; then ID=VS/RS.
  3. Apply Vi=1 V p‑p at 1 kHz. Observe Vi and Vo together: they are in phase. Measure Vo and calculate Af=Vo/Vi.
  4. From the measured Af, calculate the open-loop gain A=Af/(1−Af) and compare it with gmRS′.
  5. Zi. Use the half-voltage method with a DRB in series with the input (values near 500 kΩ). Use a ×10 probe so that the CRO does not load the high-impedance node.
  6. Zo. Remove RL and note Vo. Connect a DRB across the output and reduce it until Vo halves; the DRB setting is Zo.
  7. Optionally measure the frequency response from 20 Hz to 1 MHz.

Part B · Open-ended experiment 2

Class-C tuned amplifier

DateBatchMarksSignature

Aim

To design a class-C tuned amplifier for a resonant frequency of about 50 kHz and to study its output waveform, frequency response, bandwidth, Q factor and efficiency.

Components and equipment

#ItemSpecificationQty
1NPN transistorBC547 (2N2222 or SL100 for more power)1
2Resistors, ¼ W10 kΩ (RB), 10 Ω (RE), 10 kΩ (RL)3
3Capacitors0.1 µF ×2 (Cin, Cout), 0.01 µF (tank C1)3
4Inductor1 mH (tank L1)1
5DC supply, function generator, CRO12 V; generator to 100 kHz1 each
6DC ammeter0–50 mA, for efficiency (optional)1

Theory

Power amplifiers are classified by the conduction angle θ, the part of each input cycle during which the transistor conducts: class A 360°, class B 180°, class AB between the two, and class C less than 180° (typically 60°–120°). The less time the transistor conducts, the less power it dissipates, so class C has the highest efficiency: theoretically approaching 100 % as θ shrinks, and 60–80 % in practice.

The collector current of a class-C stage is a train of short pulses, rich in harmonics. A tuned tank L1∥C1 in the collector has a high impedance only near its resonant frequency. Each current pulse tops up the energy circulating in the tank, and the tank keeps oscillating sinusoidally between pulses (the flywheel effect). The output is therefore a sine wave at fr, and the harmonics are rejected.

fr=12πL1C1,Q=frBW,BW=f2−f1(at 0.707 of the peak output) η=PacPdc=Vo(peak)2/2RLVCCIC(dc)

Biasing. The base has no forward bias; RB returns it to ground. On each positive input peak the base-emitter junction conducts and charges Cin, which shifts the average base voltage negative (a clamping action, also called signal bias). The transistor then conducts only on the tips of the positive peaks. A larger time constant RBCin gives a smaller conduction angle.

Class-C amplifiers cannot be used for audio because the output would be badly distorted. They are used in radio transmitters, where the tank selects a single frequency, and as frequency multipliers when the tank is tuned to a harmonic.

Design

  1. Resonant frequency about 50 kHz. Choose C1=0.01 µF.L1=14π2fr2C1=14π2×(50×103)2×0.01×10−6=1.01mH→use 1mH fr=12π1×10−3×0.01×10−6=50.3kHz
  2. Input clamp, with a time constant much longer than one cycle.RB=10kΩ,Cin=0.1µF→τ=RBCin=1ms≫20µs
  3. A small emitter resistor turns the collector current pulses into a voltage for viewing.RE=10Ω→iC=vRE10Ω
  4. Output coupling with a light load, to keep the tank Q high.Cout=0.1µF(XC≈32Ω at 50kHz),RL=10kΩ
  5. Input: a sine at fr of about 4 V p‑p, enough to drive the base well past cut-in on the peaks.

Circuit diagram

Procedure

  1. Wire the circuit of Fig. B2.1. With no input and 12 V applied, the transistor is off: VC≈12 V and the supply current is nearly zero.
  2. Apply a 50 kHz, 4 V p‑p sine. Observe Vi, the voltage across RE (current pulses) and Vo on the CRO.
  3. Adjust the input frequency for maximum output. This frequency is the measured fr.
  4. From the width of the current pulses, estimate the conduction angle θ=(pulse width/T)×360°.
  5. Frequency response. Keep Vi constant and vary the frequency from 30 kHz to 75 kHz, taking finer steps near fr (Table B2.1). Plot Vo/Vo(max) against frequency, find f1 and f2 at 0.707, and calculate BW and Q.
  6. Efficiency (optional). Insert the ammeter in the 12 V lead to read IC(dc). Calculate Pdc=VCCIC(dc) and Pac=Vo(peak)2/(2RL), and hence η.

Part B · Open-ended experiment 3

Schmitt trigger for given UTP and LTP

DateBatchMarksSignature

Aim

To design an op-amp Schmitt trigger for a given upper threshold point (UTP = 4 V) and lower threshold point (LTP = 2 V), and to verify its switching action and hysteresis.

Components and equipment

#ItemSpecificationQty
1Op-ampµA7411
2Resistors, ¼ W10 kΩ (R1); 90 kΩ (R2 = 82 kΩ + 8.2 kΩ, or a 100 kΩ pot)3
3Reference3.33 V from a DC supply channel (or a 1 kΩ pot across +12 V)1
4Power supply±12 V1
5Function generator, CROtriangle wave; X-Y mode1 each

Theory

A plain comparator switches every time the input crosses the reference, so a slow or noisy input makes the output chatter. The Schmitt trigger adds positive feedback: a fraction of the output is fed back to the non-inverting input, so the switching threshold depends on the present output state. The input must rise past the upper threshold to switch one way and fall below the lower threshold to switch back. The gap between them, the hysteresis, rejects noise smaller than itself and turns any slowly varying input into a clean square wave.

In the inverting circuit used here, the input goes to the inverting terminal. R2 feeds the output back to the non-inverting terminal, which R1 ties to the reference voltage VREF:

V+=VREFR2+VoR1R1+R2 UTP=VREFR2+VsatR1R1+R2,LTP=VREFR2−VsatR1R1+R2 VH=UTP−LTP=2VsatR1R1+R2,VC=UTP+LTP2=VREFR2R1+R2

With VREF=0 the thresholds are symmetrical, ±VsatR1/(R1+R2). Because the circuit is inverting, the output goes to −Vsat when the rising input passes UTP and back to +Vsat when the falling input passes LTP.

Design

Given UTP = 4 V and LTP = 2 V. With ±12 V supplies the 741 saturates at about ±Vsat=±10 V (measure your own value).

  1. The hysteresis sets the resistor ratio.VH=4−2=2V=2×10×R1R1+R2→R1R1+R2=0.1→R2=9R1 R1=10kΩ→R2=90kΩ(82kΩ+8.2kΩ)
  2. The centre of the window sets the reference.VC=4+22=3V=VREFR2R1+R2=0.9VREF→VREF=3.33V
  3. Check.UTP=3.33×90+10×10100=4.0V,LTP=3.33×90−10×10100=2.0V✓
Open-ended. Redesign for the thresholds your instructor gives. For symmetrical thresholds of ±1 V, use VREF=0 with R2/R1=9. If VREF comes from a potentiometer, its source resistance adds to R1, so keep the pot value small (1 kΩ) or buffer it.

Circuit diagram

Procedure

  1. Wire the circuit of Fig. B3.1 with ±12 V on pins 7 and 4.
  2. Measure +Vsat and −Vsat by applying a steady ±5 V to the input. If they differ from ±10 V, recalculate R2 and VREF.
  3. Set VREF=3.33 V with the DMM.
  4. Apply a 10 V p‑p triangular wave at 100 Hz–1 kHz. Observe Vi and Vo together and note the input voltage at which the output switches from +Vsat to −Vsat (UTP) and back (LTP).
  5. Select X-Y mode (Vi on X, Vo on Y) to display the hysteresis loop. Read UTP and LTP from the loop.
  6. Repeat with VREF=0 to observe symmetrical thresholds.

Part B · Open-ended experiment 4

Sample-and-hold circuit

DateBatchMarksSignature

Aim

To design and test a sample-and-hold circuit using op-amps and a MOSFET switch, and to observe the sampling and holding of an analog signal.

Components and equipment

#ItemSpecificationQty
1Op-ampsµA741 ×2 (a JFET-input TL071 or LF356 is better for U2)2
2N-channel enhancement MOSFET2N7000 (or BS170)1
3Hold capacitor0.01 µF, polystyrene or polypropylene (low leakage)1
4Power supply±12 V1
5Function generatorsone for the signal, one for the sampling pulses (0 to +10 V)2
6CROdual channel1

Theory

An analog-to-digital converter needs its input to stay still while it converts. A sample-and-hold (S/H) circuit captures the input voltage at an instant and holds it constant for as long as needed.

  • Sample mode: the control pulse Vp is high, so the MOSFET is on with a small resistance Ron. The input buffer U1 charges the hold capacitor CH quickly to Vin, and the output follows the input.
  • Hold mode: Vp is low, the MOSFET is off, and CH keeps its charge. The output buffer U2, with its very high input impedance, reads the capacitor voltage without discharging it.
Acquisition:τ=(Ro(U1)+Ron)CH,settles in about 5τ Droop rate:dVdt=IleakCH(U2 bias current + switch leakage)

The choice of CH is a trade-off. A large CH droops less but charges slowly and needs a longer sample pulse. A small CH acquires quickly but droops faster and suffers more from the charge injected by the switch as it turns off (the hold step, or pedestal).

By the sampling theorem the sampling frequency must be at least twice the highest signal frequency (fs≥2fmax), otherwise the samples describe a lower, false frequency (aliasing). For a clear staircase on the CRO, use fs about ten times the signal frequency.

The 2N7000 has a body diode from source to drain. If the held voltage exceeds the input by more than about 0.6 V during a hold, this diode conducts and drags CH towards the input. Keeping the signal small and fs well above fin keeps the difference below that level.

Design

  1. Signal and sampling rates.Vin:1kHz sine,1V p‑p;fs=10kHz(10 samples per cycle),20% duty sample time=20µs,hold time=80µs
  2. Gate drive: the MOSFET must stay on at the most positive input.Vp=0V (off)/+10V (on);VGS(on)≥10−0.5=9.5V≫VGS(th)≈2V✓
  3. Acquisition with CH=0.01 µF.τ=(75Ω+5Ω)×0.01µF=0.8µs→5τ=4µs<20µs✓
  4. Droop with a 741 (IB≈80 nA).dVdt=80nA0.01µF=8V/s→0.64mV over an 80µs hold✓
  5. Body-diode check: the largest change of the input during one sampling period.ΔV≈2π×0.5V×1kHz×100µs≈0.31V<0.6V✓

Circuit diagram

Procedure

  1. Wire the circuit of Fig. B4.1 with ±12 V to both op-amps.
  2. Apply Vin (1 kHz, 1 V p‑p sine) and Vp (10 kHz pulses, 0 to +10 V, 20 % duty cycle).
  3. View Vin and Vo together with DC coupling. Vo follows Vin during each pulse and stays flat between pulses, giving a staircase version of the sine.
  4. Change fs to 5 kHz and 20 kHz and the duty cycle to 10 % and 50 %, and note the effect on the output (Table B4.1).
  5. Optionally lower fs below 2 kHz (less than twice fin) and observe aliasing.
  6. Optionally stop the pulses in the hold state and watch Vo drift, to estimate the droop rate.
